title: Reward changes the use and structure of predictive spatial maps
authors: Oza, S.; Cohen, A.; Wager, G.; Derdikman, D.; Recanatesi, S.
abstract: Reward-related changes in hippocampal place-cell activity may reflect either different use of an existing spatial map or plasticity that reshapes the map. We separated these contributions in a two-pathway model: a recurrent network learned to predict sensory input and developed a spatial representation, while a reinforcement-learning controller combined this representation with an explicit goal signal to guide behavior. Replaying identical trajectories before and after learning isolated representational plasticity. Goal-directed behavior strongly concentrated place fields near reward, whereas changes to the representation were smaller and more variable. A reward-proximity teaching signal made these changes larger and more consistent, and the change was strongly attenuated when recurrent plasticity was restricted. After reward relocation, goal-related directional tuning adapted more fully than place-field organization, while withdrawing reward and proximity teaching reversed the learned field concentration. Thus, reward affects predictive spatial maps through separable mechanisms: goal information changes how an existing map is used, whereas reward-related teaching signals reshape the map itself. Our results provide a concrete framework for future experiments to disentangle how reward information, plasticity and behavior jointly shape hippocampal activity.

title: Beyond Neural Noise: Critical Dynamics Predict Slower Reaction Times in Adults With and Without ADHD
authors: DallaVecchia, A.; Zink, N.; O'Connell, S. R.; Betts, S. S.; Noah, S.; Hillberg, A.; Oliva, M. T.; McCracken, J. T.; Reid, R. C.; Simpson, G. V.; Karalunas, S. L.; Calhoun, V. D.; Lenartowicz, A.
abstract: Historically, neural variability observed during task was interpreted as noise, assumed to obscure meaningful signal and thus something to be minimized both analytically by researchers and functionally by the brain. Changes to this signal-to-noise ratio have been proposed as a possible neural mechanism behind the increased reaction-time variability (RTV) in attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). However, not all variability is the same - in some cases, variability can have some underlying statistical structure that can be beneficial to information processing. The challenge lies in distinguishing meaningful variability from random noise. The edge-of-synchrony critical point, which describes a system poised between synchronous and asynchronous regimes, could be a good theoretical framework to study these different types of neural variability. In this study, we investigate whether changes in criticality and oscillatory dynamics preceded slower behavioral responses during a bimodal continuous performance task in ADHD. We find evidence that, prior to slower responses, neural dynamics shift toward criticality in both ADHD and control groups, suggesting that increase variability in ADHD and during attention lapses are related to structured variability and not necessarily random noise. Notably, these findings run counter predictions based on the proposed model and previous literature on neural noise in this population, challenging predictions of edge-of-synchrony criticality as a unifying account of neural variability and behavioral performance. Furthermore, this effect did not emerge at the between-subject level, underscoring the limitations of relying on between-subject correlations to infer neural mechanisms.

title: Multi-region two-photon calcium imaging in freely moving animals
authors: Kjellevold-Skallerud, E.; Ma, S.; Arbaciauskaite, J.; Saxena, R.; Camara, A. L.; Jenssen, K. J.; Whitlock, J. R.; Manfred, G.; Zong, W.
abstract: Complex behaviors emerge from the coordinated activity of neural circuits distributed across widely separated brain regions. Existing optical approaches for monitoring neural activity lack the combined capability to record from anatomically distributed regions with high spatiotemporal resolution in freely moving animals. Here we introduce MINI2P-II, a 1.1-g 2P miniscope that achieves large-scale calcium imaging with high spatial resolution, deep imaging depth and dual-color imaging capability. Together with a dual-scope imaging system and a novel implantable periscope lens assembly, MINI2P-II enables simultaneous 2P imaging in widely separated or anatomically adjacent brain regions. In mice, we demonstrate inter-hemisphere coordination in bilateral motor cortex during climbing, egocentric boundary coding in simultaneous retrosplenial and posterior parietal cortex recordings, and in zebra finches, we showed large-scale behavior-dependent activity in both juvenile and adult individuals. MINI2P-II opens the door to multi-region 2P imaging across species and developmental stages in freely moving animals.

title: Allosteric Biosensors Unravel GTPase-Effector Feedback
authors: Choi, M.; Ravishankar, R.; He, L.; Yan, Y.; Kreider, G. J.; Xu, P.; Lee, D. E.; Danuser, G.; Hahn, K. M.
abstract: Fluorescent biosensors that report protein conformation in vivo have been invaluable for understanding how the spatio-temporal dynamics of signaling controls cells. However, for GTPases these biosensors report the activated conformation using reagents that block the binding of downstream proteins, generating dominant negative effects and altering normal cell physiology. We present here a generalizable design to make GTPase biosensors (AlloRac1 and AlloCdc42), in which a circularly permuted fluorescent protein is inserted into a conserved loop allosterically connected to the effector binding site, generating activity-dependent fluorescence without blocking ligand interactions. The Rac1 biosensor showed that effector interactions led to increased Rac1 activation, indicating an auto-regulatory positive feedback made visible by the new biosensor design. This feedback regulated the kinetics and localization of Rac1 activity, including Rac1 activity gradients that controlled motility. Feedback was generated through Rac1 interaction with the effector Pak1, which led to further activation of Rac1 by the guanine exchange factor {beta}-Pix. The new biosensor approach enables quantitative imaging of previously obscure spatio-temporal dynamics in GTPase regulation.

title: Interpreting Short Tandem Repeat Variations with Genomic Foundation Models in Olive
authors: Xia, F.; Pakdel, M. H.; Mazinani, M. H.; Asadi, A.; Zeng, Y.; Zhang, J.; Shariati, V.; Anisimova, M.
abstract: Short tandem repeats (STRs) are highly mutable, multiallelic variants with distinctive mutation dynamics and have been associated with phenotypic variation across diverse species. However, genome-wide STR variation remains poorly characterized in olive, and the large number of naturally occurring alleles creates a challenge for variant interpretation. Genomic language models offer a potential way to assess how STR length changes alter learned sequence representations, but their responses to natural multiallelic STR series have not been systematically evaluated. Here, we identified 117,119 polymorphic STRs across 212 Iranian and Mediterranean olive accessions. STRs recovered the major SNP-defined ancestry axes while resolving additional geographically structured subcomponents. We then quantified STR-induced embedding perturbation using three plant genomic language models: AgroNT, PlantCAD2, and GPN. Across all three models, embedding distance generally increased with repeat-length difference from the reference allele, and 7,417 loci were embedding-sensitive in all three models. These signals were robust to fixed-length input construction and exceeded those of matched nonrepetitive indels at most tested loci. Integration with oil-composition associations prioritized four exploratory loci supported by all three models. Overall, we provide a genome-wide olive STR resource and show that plant genomic language models capture reproducible responses to natural STR length variation. Combining cross-model embedding evidence with phenotype association provides a potential framework for prioritizing candidate STRs for further investigation.

title: Transcranial electrical stimulation for memory enhancement: A systematic review and meta-analysis
authors: Goto, Y.; Onagawa, R.; Takemi, M.; Ishikawa, K.; Narukawa, S.; Amano, K.; Hosomi, K.
abstract: Non-invasive brain stimulation techniques have received increasing interest for their potential to enhance memory function, a fundamental cognitive aspect of daily life. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to investigate the efficacy of transcranial electrical stimulation (tES) in enhancing memory function in healthy adults, following the pre-registered strategy at PROSPERO (CRD42022353630). A total of 113 articles (193 trials, 7,299 participants) examining tES were identified. Meta- analysis revealed a significant overall effect of tES on memory function compared with sham stimulation (standardised mean difference [95% confidence interval] = 0.19 [0.12, 0.25]). A positive pooled effect was also observed in the subgroup receiving frontal transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS). Stimulation was associated with positive pooled effects for working- and declarative-memory task performance. Significant pooled effects were observed within 1 day after stimulation; longer-term estimates were imprecise. Regarding adverse events, tingling and itching sensations on the scalp occurred more frequently in the active group than in the sham group, but no serious adverse events were reported. Limitations, including small- study effects, heterogeneity, and uneven coverage of memory domains, were noted, emphasising the need for improved experimental rigour and diversification of memory tasks. These findings suggest that tES is associated with small improvements in memory-task performance and was generally well tolerated under the studied protocols. Heterogeneity, small- study effects, and limited adverse-event reporting constrain conclusions about efficacy, durability, and safety

title: Geometry shapes cytoplasmic Cdk1 waves that drive cortical dynamics
authors: Cebrian-Lacasa, D.; Leda, M.; Goryachev, A.; Gelens, L.
abstract: Cell division in large embryos is coordinated by spatial waves of Cyclin B-Cdk1 activity that spread through the cytoplasm and drive cortical contractility. However, it remains unclear how cell size and nuclear enrichment of Cyclin B-Cdk1 shape these waves, and how the cytoplasmic signal is transmitted to the cortex. Here we couple established reaction-diffusion models of Cyclin B-Cdk1 signaling and the excitable Rho-actin cortex to ask how cell geometry and elevated nuclear Cyclin B-Cdk1 concentration shape cytoplasmic wave propagation in spherical cells. We find that cytoplasmic waves consist of two distinct parts: an activation front that propagates in a manner consistent with trigger-wave behavior, and a wave back controlled by concentration gradients in the cell cycle oscillator. Because these parts are generated by different mechanisms, they can move at different speeds or even in opposite directions, depending on nuclear size and effective cell size. This yields a simple geometric explanation for why surface contraction waves propagate in opposite directions in starfish oocytes and Xenopus embryos, without invoking system-specific cortical mechanisms. Coupling the Cdk1 signal to the cortex further shows how cytoplasmic waveforms regulate Rho-actin dynamics through inhibition of the Rho GEF Ect2. Together, these results provide a mechanistic framework linking localized nuclear activation, cytoplasmic Cdk1 waves, and cortical responses in large embryonic cells.

title: Meiotic null MSH2 and SGS1 alleles in S. cerevisiae x S. uvarum hybrids result in near-haploid offspring with mixed parental chromosomal inheritance
authors: Wang, T. K.; Dunham, M. J.
abstract: In the natural world, genetic isolation between closely related species is often maintained by direct F1 hybrid sterility or hybrid breakdown in subsequent generations. This phenomenon is also observed in microorganisms within species of the Saccharomyces clade, including the model organism Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Members of Saccharomyces intermate and historical hybridization events have left genomic footprints, but these hybrids are themselves sterile and produce very few viable offspring. Previous work suggests a main cause of F1 hybrid sterility is the action of mismatch repair machinery. The sequence divergence between two parent Saccharomyces species--from ~10% to ~20%--is recognized by the cell as an aberrant attempt to recombine nonhomologous chromosomes during meiosis I, leading to massive nondisjunction and aneuploidy. Deletion of mismatch repair machinery improves fertility in hybrids of S. cerevisiae and its sister species S. paradoxus but leads to increased mutation accumulation during normal mitotic growth. To overcome this drawback, conditional alleles that specifically repress expression of mismatch repair machinery during meiosis have been applied in S. cerevisiae x S. paradoxus hybrids with success. Here, we describe the application of the meiotic null system to a different hybrid: S. cerevisiae x S. uvarum. The system does not increase hybrid fertility likely due to increased sequence divergence and chromosomal translocations, but mass spore recovery and flow cytometry enable the recovery of near-haploid offspring which inherit an assortment of parental chromosomes. These populations of mixed hybrid genomes can be leveraged in phenotypic studies to further understand the effects of hybrid genomes on organismal fitness.

title: GBactPro: cross-species bacterial promoter prediction using element-resolved promoter definitions
authors: Han, H.-Y. B.; Kao, Y.-C. V.; Kuo, S.-T. A.; Chou, H.-H. D.; Chang, J.-M.
abstract: Accurate bacterial promoter prediction supports genome annotation, but many models use fixed-length promoter windows anchored to transcription start sites (TSSs) rather than promoter-element boundaries. We developed the General Bacterial Promoter Predictor (GBactPro), a convolutional neural network-bidirectional long short-term memory (CNN-BiLSTM) framework using promoter sequences resolved by the Promoter Architecture Scanner. Using Escherichia coli-trained models evaluated across 43 bacterial species, we compared eight input designs and identified the contiguous -35/spacer/-10 core as optimal (mean AUROC = 0.9859). Species-specific models showed broad transfer in a 43 x 43 evaluation. Joint training on all 43 species achieved a mean AUROC of 0.9943 across their held-out test sets and outperformed four established predictors under matched-length benchmarks. In genome-wide E. coli scanning, GBactPro achieved AUROC and AUPRC values of 0.979 and 0.160 under stringent full-containment matching (0-bp tolerance), increasing to 0.997 and 0.323 under a 100-bp tolerance. False-positive predictions overlapped H-NS binding regions more frequently than true positives (24.4% versus 18.8%), and predictions also overlapped promoters derepressed in an H-NS-knockout dataset. Prediction precision varied across four TSS classes. These findings demonstrate that element-resolved promoter definitions improve cross-species prediction and support genome-wide identification of candidate bacterial promoters.

title: A multispecies foundation model for genome function prediction, gene annotation and sequence design
authors: Boshar, S.; Evans, B.; Tang, Z.; Adel, Y.; Bornachot, Y.; Sidbon, S.; Lorbeer, F. K.; Picard, A.; Rajesh, C.; Seitz, E.; Emms, D.; Mendoza-Revilla, J.; Hernandez, A.; Al-Ani, F.; Karch, T.; Schiff, Y.; Lopez, M.; Laterre, A.; Beguir, K.; Koo, P.; Kuleshov, V.; Stark, A.; de Almeida, B. P.; Pierrot, T.
abstract: Comparative genomics and synthetic biology require models that can interpret, annotate, and design DNA sequences across species, yet genomic models have not combined these capabilities beyond a few well-characterized organisms. Here we introduce Nucleotide Transformer v3 (NTv3), a long-context cross-kingdom foundation model that provides a common backbone for functional prediction, gene annotation and controllable sequence generation across phylogenetically diverse species. NTv3 is pre-trained on more than 128,000 genomes using sequences up to 1Mb and post-trained on 16,262 functional tracks across 15 animal and plant genomes. NTv3 performs comparably to AlphaGenome on matched human assays and matches or exceeds evaluated published models for functional-track prediction across 19 species spanning mammals, birds, fish, plants, fungi and protists. Ablation experiments show that both genome pre-training and expanding functional supervision from human and mouse to 15 species improve track prediction. Leveraging these learned functional representations, NTv3 outperforms leading ab initio gene predictors across mammals, plants and insects, with fewer spurious gene models and improved recovery and reduced fragmentation of long genes. Finally, the same representations can be used with discrete diffusion to design regulatory DNA sequences with specific activity levels. We demonstrate this in plant and fly promoters and enhancers, and experimentally validate the activity and promoter selectivity of the generated fly enhancers. Together, NTv3 unifies genome interpretation, gene annotation and regulatory sequence design across the animal and plant kingdoms, with direct relevance to agriculture, biodiversity research and biotechnology.

title: CellMethMarker provides an integrated database of human cell- and tissue-type-specific DNA methylation markers
authors: Sun, X.; Peng, Y.; Yi, Y.; Fu, L.; Liu, F.; Xie, Y.; Dai, Q.; Gu, H.; Shi, J.; Wang, H.; Zhang, F.
abstract: Cell- and tissue-type-specific DNA methylation markers provide epigenetic signatures of cellular identity and are widely used to infer cellular origin from bulk and single-cell methylomes. Existing resources mainly emphasize disease-associated biomarkers, methylome atlases, genomic annotations or RNA-based cell markers, leaving an unmet need for an integrated region-level resource dedicated to such markers. Here we present CellMethMarker (http://gu-zhanglab.hfcas.ac.cn/CellMethMarker), a curated database integrating 347,514 de novo markers derived from uniformly processed whole-genome and reduced-representation bisulfite sequencing datasets, 2,203,507 literature-derived marker records and harmonized metadata for 2,810 samples. CellMethMarker enables cell- and tissue-centered marker retrieval, coordinate-based search, genome-browser visualization, interactive methylation analysis and data download. In an independent single-cell methylome atlas, these markers recover the expected cell-type-associated methylation patterns, and a platform-matched reference built from them lowers the mean deconvolution error from 0.365 to 0.144. CellMethMarker therefore links region-level DNA methylation variation to cellular identity and supports methylome-based cell-type annotation and deconvolution.

title: Informed, scalable and unified transport couplings for single-cell alignment and downstream inference with scBIOT
authors: Zhang, H.; Qin, P.
abstract: Single-cell genomics requires methods that account for technical variation while preserving biological signals, remain tractable at atlas scale and support analyses beyond visualization, but existing approaches discard the fitted correspondence that could connect these tasks. Here we introduce scBIOT, a biologically informed optimal-transport framework that formulates single-cell alignment as an explicit and inspectable coupling between cells. scBIOT incorporates prior biological knowledge to preserve known cell identities, compresses transport through prototypes for large datasets and quantifies gene-level changes induced by alignment using coupling-derived transport scores. Across transcriptomic and spatial mapping benchmarks, scBIOT balanced biological conservation, batch correction and label-transfer accuracy while distinguishing batch-associated stress responses from biological immune and drug-response programs. Prototype transport scaled coupling-based analysis to approximately 100 million perturbed cells. Because the coupling encodes probabilistic correspondences rather than only corrected coordinates, the same fitted coupling supports state mapping, trajectory inference, perturbation analysis, multimodal comparison and spatiotemporal localization. Applications to cancer, hematopoiesis and embryonic development identified condition-specific cell states, modality-dependent regulatory programs and spatially resolved developmental transitions. Informed, scalable and unified transport couplings therefore link atlas alignment to downstream biological inference within a single framework.

title: HOMED enables hierarchical and multimodal optimization of DNA methylation deconvolution across tissues
authors: Liu, Y.; Chen, Y.; Du, Y.; Garmire, L.
abstract: Cellular heterogeneity is a major confounder in bulk DNA methylation data for epigenome-wide association studies. Existing reference-based DNAm deconvolution methods often ignore hierarchies among related cell types and may generalize poorly across datasets due to limited variability in reference profiles. We developed HOMED (Hierarchically Optimized Methylation Deconvolution), a framework that integrates cell-lineage hierarchies, single-cell RNA sequencing-guided deconvolution, and paired bulk RNA-seq/DNAm data for CpG signature optimization. Across simulated and real peripheral blood mononuclear cell, lung, and placental datasets, HOMED consistently yielded the highest PCCs and lowest RMSEs, outperforming existing scRNA-seq-guided DNAm deconvolution methods, improving accuracy, resolution, and cross-tissue generalizability.

title: A mechanistic classification of GNAO1 mutations links Gβ γ sequestration to hyperkinetic disease and treatment response
authors: Soden, G.; Robichaux-Viehoever, A.; Soden, K.; Laux, J.; Dohlman, H. G.; Christoffel, D.
abstract: Go is the most prevalent G protein subunit in the brain and is critical for signal transduction through G protein-coupled receptors. Mutations in the gene encoding Go (GNAO1) cause a rare neurodevelopmental disorder with involuntary movements (NEDIM) and, in some patients, developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE). Here, we integrate human genetic analysis with cellular assays to define mechanistic classes of GNAO1 mutations and in vivo approaches to evaluate therapeutic strategies. We grouped variants into two functional categories: those predicted to sequester G{beta}{gamma} and those with reduced Go expression and therefore increased G{beta}{gamma} signaling. Analysis of patient data revealed that mutations predicted to impair G{beta}{gamma} release are significantly associated with NEDIM. Using the GNAO1R209H/+ mouse as a model of NEDIM, we evaluated two small molecules: caffeine, a nonselective adenosine receptor antagonist, and gallein, a selective modulator of G{beta}{gamma}-effector interactions. Both compounds significantly reduced hyperlocomotion in the open field test. Whole-cell patch-clamp electrophysiology revealed sex- and cell type-specific hyperexcitability in spiny projection neurons within the dorsolateral striatum of GNAO1R209H/+ mice. Together, these findings implicate dysfunction of dorsolateral striatal pathways in GNAO1-related disorder and suggest that mechanistic understanding of disease variants can guide targeted therapeutic strategies.

title: How goals shape naturalistic memories: bias in gaze and narrative recall
authors: Habenicht, H.; Mueller, M.; Schoenauer, M.; Roueast, N. M.
abstract: Episodic memories are thought to represent information framed by our individual perception and goals, yet personal experiences are hard to evaluate externally. Due to novel methodological advances, we could now trace the development of such goal-shaped memories in a naturalistic experimental setting. We recorded eye-tracking while participants encoded episodic-like memories, and later recorded participants freely narrating their experiences. Naturalistic goal-states were induced by introducing a secret job, which promised to reward participants later for person-based or space-based information. Using computer-vision based semantic segmentation of visual scanning behaviour in movie scenes and data-driven coding of free recall performance, we show that these goals increasingly shift attention during memory encoding and systematically bias narration during retrieval to goal-relevant dimensions. Our findings highlight that we can use data-driven methodology to observe how naturally occurring or induced biases shape how we perceive and remember the world.

title: NeuroMark-SZ: A Holistic Resting-State-fMRI-Based Model for Divergent Functional Circuitry in Schizophrenia
authors: Jensen, K. M.; Ballem, R.; Kinsey, S.; Andres-Camazon, P.; Fu, Z.; Chen, J.; Haas, S. S.; Diaz-Caneja, C. M.; Bustillo, J. R.; Preda, A.; van Erp, T. G. M.; Pearlson, G.; Kochunov, P.; Turner, J. A.; Calhoun, V. D.; Iraji, A.
abstract: Background: Schizophrenia is a severe neuropsychiatric disorder. Efforts to describe the underlying biology and establish diagnostic markers through non-invasive neuroimaging methods are ongoing, resulting in a range of theoretical brain-based frameworks. Prominent frameworks for aberrant schizophrenia-associated functional connectivity in resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rsfMRI) include the dysconnectivity hypothesis, theory of cognitive dysmetria, and triple network theory. Although informative, prior work can be improved by increasing sample size, avoiding confirmation bias, and accounting for individual variability and the effects of medication and chronicity. Methods: With these recommendations in mind, we employed a data-driven, whole-brain approach using a large multi-site rsfMRI dataset (N = 2,656; schizophrenia = 1,248). We used reference-guided independent component analysis to generate subject-specific whole-brain functional network connectivity (FNC) and extract imaging markers of similarity to schizophrenia patterns. We modeled the relationship between medication dosage, age of onset, chronicity, symptom severity, and cognitive performance and FNC. Results: Our analysis identified a reliable schizophrenia-FNC signature characterized by aberrantly stronger negative cerebellothalamic and positive thalamocortical connectivity, implicating sensory, motor, and associative cortical circuits. While medication and chronicity were significantly associated with these signatures, the core cerebellothalamic disruptions remained a robust marker of schizophrenia. Conclusions: This work represents the largest schizophrenia-specific rsfMRI study to date, refines existing theoretical frameworks with a more nuanced map of how clinical variables interact with brain connectivity, and provides a high-fidelity template of schizophrenia-related connectivity. We have released this template as an open-access resource to facilitate reproducibility and accelerate the development of reliable rsfMRI-based schizophrenia biomarkers.

title: Polyaxonal A1 amacrine cells form a spatially extended network in primate retina
authors: Boniec, S. A.; Rieke, F.; Manookin, M.
abstract: Inhibitory networks shape information processing in the brain by integrating signals across space, regulating neuronal responses, and controlling the flow of signals through neural circuits. Understanding these computations requires linking the structure of individual inhibitory neuron types to their functional properties and network connectivity. The retina provides a tractable system for meeting this challenge, yet the organization of many retinal inhibitory circuits remains poorly understood. Here, we identify a population of polyaxonal amacrine cells recorded using multielectrode arrays as A1 amacrine cells, a morphologically defined interneuron type in primate retina. This identification is supported by a correspondence between properties of morphologically-identified A1 cells from single cell recordings and putative A1 amacrines in the array recordings. We then identified recursive bistratified ganglion cells in the array recordings based on their electrical coupling to A1 cells, linking this inhibitory network to retinal output pathways. A1 and recursive bistratified cells also share an asymmetry in receptive-field organization, with larger On than Off centers. Finally, A1 spike amplitudes decline during bursts, and analyses of their electrical images suggest that this change may cause some spikes to fail to propagate through their extensive axonal arbors. These findings establish the cellular identity and network organization of a long-range inhibitory circuit in the primate retina and reveal how neuronal architecture, connectivity, and spike dynamics may jointly shape the transmission of visual information.

title: Spontaneous neural activity in the developing ant olfactory system
authors: Frank, D. D.; Kronauer, D. J. C.
abstract: Spontaneous neural activity is a pillar of mammalian neurodevelopment. In mammals, developing olfactory sensory neurons (OSNs) show spontaneous activity patterns that depend on the olfactory receptor (OR) they express. This activity is necessary for proper sorting of OSN axons into olfactory bulb glomeruli. This contrasts with the simpler olfactory system of the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster, where antennal lobe glomeruli form without functional ORs. Compared to Drosophila, ants have a vastly expanded olfactory system and, unlike Drosophila, require functional ORs for proper development. This raises the possibility that ants, like mammals, rely on spontaneous neural activity. To test whether developing ant OSNs are spontaneously active, we performed live calcium imaging in translucent pupae of the clonal raider ant Ooceraea biroi, using a transgenic line expressing the genetically encoded calcium indicator GCaMP6s in OSNs. Developing O. biroi OSNs exhibit spontaneous calcium transients from the earliest stages of glomerulus formation, and features of this activity change over the course of metamorphosis. During early stages, activity is faster, varies widely between cells, and is uncorrelated across the OSN population. By mid-metamorphosis, activity has slowed, with longer calcium events and fewer peaks per cell. As pupae approach eclosion, a new mode appears, with rhythmic, sawtooth-shaped calcium events that synchronously engage OSNs in both antennae. This stage-dependent spontaneous activity suggests that the expanded ant olfactory system may use a developmental logic more akin to mammals than to Drosophila.

title: The TREM-receptor family interactome in the human brain
authors: de Kleijn, K.; Weller, S.; Klaassen, R.; Koopmans, F.; Smit, A.; Wijdeven, R.
abstract: The Triggering Receptors Expressed on Myeloid cells (TREMs) are a family of cell-surface receptors instrumental in the activation of different myeloid cells. TREM2, its most studied member, is genetically linked to Alzheimer disease (AD), and its interactions with BAmyloid; and APOE have placed it at the forefront of microglia dysfunction in the brain. However, the ligands and binding partners of the other TREM members (TREM1, TREML1, TREML2 and TREML4) are less well defined. Here, we used human AD and non-AD brain lysate to profile the interactome of the ligand binding domains of the different TREM receptors. Besides identifying known ligands for TREM1 (PGLYRP1), TREM2 (C1QL3, LGALSL) and TREML1 (Fibrinogens), we identified complement components and the apolipoproteins APOA1 and APOA4 as novel interactors of TREML1, and heparan sulfate modified proteins as binding partners for TREML2. Furthermore, similar to TREM2, all the TREMLs interacted with the apolipoproteins APOE and Clusterin. Using in vitro pulldowns with heparin, we confirmed that specifically TREML2 interacted with heparan sulfates, in a manner unaffected by the AD-linked S144G mutation. Together, our proteomics approach identified novel interactors for TREML1 and TREML2, cementing the role of the different TREM-proteins in lipid trafficking and immunity.

title: Neuroprotective activity of sub-anesthetic ketamine in a preclinical model of Parkinson's disease is not blocked by antagonizing brain-derived neurotrophic factor signaling
authors: Stopera, C. J.; Bartlett, M. J.; Bernard, K.; Conklin, R.; Singh, S.; Frye, J.; Madhavan, L.; Doyle, K. P.; Sherman, S. J.; Steece-Collier, K.; Falk, T.
abstract: Treatment with low-dose ketamine is neuroprotective in rodent models of acute damage, while high doses of ketamine can be neurotoxic. Our group has previously shown that sub-anesthetic ketamine treatment leads to long-term reduction of L-DOPA-induced dyskinesia (LID) via brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF)-signaling in a rat 6-hydroxydopamine (6-OHDA) model of Parkinson's disease (PD). In this report, we investigated if sub-anesthetic ketamine is also neuroprotective in a progressive 6-OHDA model of PD via neurotrophic action through the tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB) receptor. We demonstrated that ketamine-treatment (20 mg/kg, i.p.) prior to striatal administration of the neurotoxin 6-OHDA is neuroprotective, providing near complete protection against development of parkinsonian motor deficits. This robust behavioral efficacy occurred in the presence of only modest preservation of tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) striatal levels (~50-60% loss). Interestingly, based on data from an additional cohort treated with ketamine and ANA-12 (TrkB antagonist) we found that the neuroprotective effects of ketamine are not mediated by TrkB receptors. Semi-quantitative western analysis showed that the relative tyrosine hydroxylase content in the striatum was not significantly increased in ketamine-treated rats compared to vehicle. Unbiased stereology of dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) revealed no significant differences between any of the groups. The role of BDNF was evaluated with in situ hybridization for RNA of BDNF and TrkB. While BDNF expression was not changed, co-administration of ketamine and ANA-12 led to a significant decrease in TrkB receptor expression compared to ketamine-only on the lesioned but not the intact hemisphere in the SNc. In conclusion, we show that ketamine at the low dose currently pursued for therapeutic benefit for LID led to robust behavioral motor improvement in this rodent PD degeneration model, yet these protective effects were not driven by neurotrophic BDNF-signaling, indicating complex mechanisms are underlying neuroprotective activities of low-dose ketamine.

title: L-DOPA Rescues Reach Height but Not Trajectory Area in a Bimanual String-Pulling Behavior in Parkinsonian Rats
authors: Schmit, M. B.; Aristieta, A.; Caparu, R.; Malik, A. J.; White, A.; Surtchev, Y.; Pederson, V.; Bartlett, M. J.; Vishwanath, A.; Falk, T.; Cowen, S. L.
abstract: While gross motor changes in Parkinson's disease, bradykinesia, hypokinesia, difficulty initiating movement, have been well studied in rodent models of the disease, limb movements, and especially bimanual coordination deficits, are more difficult to study in these animal models. Here we describe a novel bimanual string-pulling task that can be used to generate a rich repertoire of behaviors that require limb and bimanual coordination in rats with unilateral 6-hydroxydopamine (6-OHDA) lesion. We show that 6-OHDA lesion significantly reduces string speed, pulling bout duration, paw speed especially during reaching, and reduces the area of paw trajectories during pulling. However, it does not affect the variability around that movement trajectory. We also show that levodopa (L-DOPA) treatment restores many of these measures but not all. L-DOPA restores paw speed and string-pulling speed and fully restores paw reach height and pulling bout duration, but has no effect on trajectory area. Together, our results demonstrate that dopamine depletion differentially effects features of this bimanual coordination task, that L-DOPA mostly, but not fully, restores string pulling performance, and opens up a new avenue for measuring the effect of Parkinson's disease treatments on motor movement, allowing for better assessment of how effectively treatments restore motor activity.

title: Brain state locks silent memories in a trained fly connectome
authors: Wang, H.; Yeong, J. P. S.; Zhao, Y.; Zhao, Y.; Yu, Z.; Liu, X.; He, R.; Chen, H.; Liu, T.; Tian, Y.; Chen, W.; Cai, Y.; Xu, Y.; Ning, H.; Hou, X.; Pang, L.; Jiang, D.; Liu, H.; Hao, J.; Tian, C.
abstract: Complete connectomes now exist for insect nervous systems, but whether a fixed wiring diagram can learn, and what its memories consist of, is unknown. Here, we trained a spiking model of the whole male Drosophila central nervous system, 167,106 neurons with fixed wiring, to plan moves and to remember a visual cue. Spikes write the cue into neuronal adaptation, which holds it silently until the next input reads it out. Cells that hold the trace are enriched for transcripts of a calcium-activated potassium channel in fly cell atlases. The learned readout recalls the trace only in the brain state of learning: the same trace evokes a different response at another delay, and a disease-like loss of potassium current rewrites the trace and changes how it is read. Learning in the new state is spared. Memory failure can arise from a change of state rather than a loss of storage.

title: Integrative drug discovery for Parkinson disease with DIMER
authors: Guo, S.; Yang, X.; Dong, Y.; Yu, L.; Sangjizhuoma, A.; Sie, K. L.; Zhu, K.; Zhang, Y.; Zhao, X.; Kerman, E.; Li, R.; He, J.
abstract: Translating Parkinson disease (PD) genetics into therapeutic candidates requires approaches that account for interconnected disease mechanisms and their cellular context. Here we present DIMER (Direct and Indirect Module Evaluation for Repurposing and screening), a framework that connects network-based drug repurposing and target-directed virtual screening through shared disease-associated gene sets. Applying DIMER to PD, we integrated genetic risk and mechanism-associated gene sets with drug-target interactions, disease transcriptomes, and single nucleus expression profiles. Network analysis identified 423 repurposing candidates, with 71% of qualifying drug-gene set associations arising through targets outside the corresponding disease gene set. Transcriptional reversal analysis and cell type-resolved networks further distinguished candidates by their predicted effects on disease-associated expression and their cellular context, while target-set separation nominated potentially complementary drug combinations. For target-directed virtual screening, DIMER adapted a pretrained compound-protein interaction model to screening library chemistry and incorporated known-ligand similarity into compound ranking. Library adaptation improved compound-target pair classification performance, whereas ligand-informed ranking increased early enrichment of known active compounds. Consensus screening of 1.82 million compounds against seven PD-associated proteins yielded a shortlist of 22 compounds supported by at least five ranking runs. In a complementary experimental evaluation, four repurposing candidates (polydatin, fedratinib, sorafenib and venlafaxine) attenuated the loss of dopamine neuron marker signals in human midbrain organoids exposed to 6-hydroxydopamine. Together, these findings establish DIMER as a framework for translating disease-associated genes into pharmacological hypotheses and prioritizing candidates for experimental testing.

title: Sex differences in latent inhibition and their implications for psychotic disorders
authors: Mawson, E. R.; Hall, J.; Thomas, K. L.
abstract: Latent inhibition (LI) refers to the reduced ability to learn or express learning about a stimulus following prior exposure to it without consequence. It has been extensively studied to investigate associative learning and memory as well as the aberrant attribution of salience to irrelevant stimuli in both humans and animals, a process which is thought to underpin hallucinations and delusions in psychosis. Despite sex differences observed in numerous aspects of psychosis, few studies have attempted to characterise sex differences in LI. This systematic review outlines the current evidence of sex differences in LI in both human and rodent studies, showing predominantly inconclusive and conflicting evidence for sex differences. However, the majority of cases in which sex differences were found were in studies that assessed the impact of additional factors on LI such as drug administration, juvenile handling, and oestrous phase, and demonstrated interactions between sex and these additional factors. Hence, there is stronger evidence for sex differences in vulnerability to perturbations in LI. Furthermore, we present data demonstrating sex differences in latent inhibition of contextual fear conditioning and associated gene expression in the hippocampus in rodents, suggesting sex differences in hippocampal processing underpinning latent inhibition at both the behavioural and neurobiological levels. Although there have been relatively few studies demonstrating sex differences in LI identified by the systematic review, the data suggest that in hippocampally dependent forms of LI, sex differences may be more apparent, which may be of relevance in relation to sex differences in the presentation of psychosis.

title: Repetitive Levodopa Treatment Drives Cell Type-Specific Striatal Adaptations Associated With Progressive Dyskinesia in Parkinsonian Mice
authors: Paz, R. M.; Ryan, M. B.; Marcott, P. F.; Girasole, A. E.; Faryean, J.; Duong, V.; Sridhar, S.; Nelson, A. B.
abstract: The use of levodopa to manage Parkinsons disease (PD) symptoms leads to levodopa-induced dyskinesia (LID) and other motor fluctuations, which worsen with disease progression and repeated treatment. Aberrant activity of striatal D1- and D2-expressing medium spiny neurons (D1-/D2-MSNs) underlies LID, but the mechanisms driving its progression remain unclear. Using the 6-OHDA mouse model of PD/LID, we combined in vivo and ex vivo recordings to isolate the effect of repeated treatment in LID worsening and other changes in the motor response to levodopa. We found that LID worsening is linked to potentiation of levodopa-evoked responses in both D1-/D2-MSNs, independent of changes in dopamine release or MSN intrinsic excitability. Instead, strengthening of glutamatergic synapses onto D1-MSNs emerged as a key signature. Moreover, we found changes in D2-MSN activity are associated with LID duration, which paralleled a reduction in D2R sensitivity. These findings reveal striatal adaptations contributing to worsening of levodopa-related complications.
